text.p: Europe's biggest mobile phone maker Nokia Oy on Thursday reported 1996 profit fell in line with market expectations but raised its dividend and said it expected strong growth and profitability to continue in 1997.

Nokia said profit before tax and minority interests fell 21 percent to 3.90 billion markka ($786 million) from 4.93 billion in 1995, recovering clearly in the second half after logistical problems in its fast-growing mobile business hit first-half earnings.

Operating profit in the fourth quarter, at 1.74 billion markka, was over 70 percent better than the fourth quarter of 1995: "That, we are very, very pleased with," CEO Jorma Ollila told a news conference.

The result was almost bang on the median of analysts' forecasts for a 3.85 billion markka profit in a 3.30-4.92 billion range, and Nokia sweetened the news by proposing a dividend of 3.50 markka, up from 3.00 markka last year.

During Helsinki hours Nokia's stock, also traded in the United States and often driven by investors there, held most earlier gains in hefty volumes after the news, but some analysts said investors may want to take profits.

"We've been buyers of the stock," said Richard Kramer at Goldman Sachs in London. "I wouldn't be surprised to see some investors wanting to take profits -- it depends on the tone of the conference call (due later on Thursday)."
Nokia's stock has climbed over 200 percent in six months, to approach a 340.00 markka life-high set in September 1995 before investor confidence was hit by Nokia's problems in mobiles.
"They're excellent figures," said Neil Barton at Merrill Lynch in London, in an initial response to the results.
He has had a "strong buy" recommendation on Nokia for some time, and without naming a target noted the stock had yet to revisit 340.00 markka.
Nokia's total net sales rose to 39.32 billion markka from 36.81 billion. Sales in telecommunications infrastructure rose 29 percent, while mobile phones sales grew by 34 percent.

"On an overall basis, we believe that we are well positioned to exploit new opportunities during 1997 and that Nokia will continue to demonstrate strong growth and good profitability," Ollila said in a statement.
"At the end of 1996, we were the global market leader in digital mobile phones, one of the largest suppliers of GSM networks, and the world's leading supplier of DCS 1800 systems," he said.

But for some analysts speaking ahead of the conference call, a potential cloud on the horizon was evidence of tighter margins in the infrastructure business, seen as a key engine of profitability as new rivals crowd handset markets.
Nokia's operating profit margin on infrastructure fell to 22 percent in 1996 from 26 percent in 1995.
Ollila said Nokia did not see any major change in the growth picture this year, and said Nokia had almost been able to match price erosion by increasing productivity.
On mobile margins, knocked by the logistics problems below seven percent over full-year 1996, Ollila said Nokia was confident of returning to the 10 percent margin of 1995.
"Our target for this year is at least 10 percent. We feel good about achieving that," he said. Nokia's second half profit margin on mobiles was 13 percent, he said.
Asked if Nokia had lost market share to any rivals, such as Sweden's Ericsson or Motorola of the U.S., he said: "I don't think we have lost to anybody." ($ = 4.961 Finnish Markka)
